data.title: Multi-objective antibody design and optimization using machine learning
data.abstract: Antibodies, ranging from conventional immunoglobulins to single-domain and bispecific antibodies, are developed for a wide spectrum of therapeutic and diagnostic applications. However, lead antibodies are commonly engineered to optimize one or more key properties, including affinity, specificity, polyreactivity, stability, aggregation, and immunogenicity, and tradeoffs among these attributes frequently hinder the development of variants suitable for clinical use. Furthermore, identifying lead candidates with desirable properties typically requires multiple rounds of experimental screening and evaluation, particularly when targeting pre-selected epitopes or challenging, high-value targets such as G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), ion channels, and multipass membrane proteins. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods can streamline experimental screening and antibody generation methods. In this Review, we discuss both computational multi-objective optimization of existing antibodies and de novo antibody design. The application of AI/ML methods has the potential to overcome current bottlenecks in antibody development and accelerate the generation of improved therapeutics for human health.
data.fulltext:
## INTRODUCTION

Therapeutic antibodies are among the most popular drugs on the market, with a combined market value of hundreds of billions of dollars. Blockbuster antibody drugs such as trastuzumab, adalimumab, pembrolizumab, and nivolumab have advanced the treatment of cancers, inflammatory diseases, infectious diseases, and more. Monoclonal antibodies are the gold standard of antibody drugs owing to their high affinity for specific antigens, enabling their use as therapeutics and in diagnostic tests.

Conventional methods of generating monoclonal antibodies include in vivo methods, such as hybridoma technology and single B cell screening, and in vitro methods, such as phage and yeast-surface display. Hybridoma technology involves immunizing animals with a target antigen, isolating antibody-producing B cells, and fusing them to immortalized cell lines to create cells capable of producing monoclonal antibodies at scale. The resultant antibodies typically require humanization, although the use of humanized transgenic mice enables the generation of fully human antibodies. Single B-cell screening, which isolates antigen-specific B cells and recovers paired heavy- and/or light-chain sequences for recombinant expression, enables the discovery of animal-derived antibodies after immunization or human antibodies from human blood. In vitro display technologies, such as phage display, yeast display, ribosomal display, and mammalian display, leverage large antibody libraries and directed evolution to discover desirable binders. After antibody discovery, lead candidates are evaluated and typically optimized for multiple properties, including expression, humanness, immunogenicity, chemical and physical stability, and specificity.

In addition to monoclonal antibodies, antibodies with non-standard formats, including heavy-chain-only antibodies and multispecific antibodies, have entered the market and are being developed using similar processes. For example, VHHs (nanobody® variants) are heavy-chain-only antibodies derived from the variable region of camelid antibodies and can be generated from immunizing camelids or from synthetic or immune VHH libraries. Owing to their small size (~15 kDa) and convex binding surface, VHHs can bind to recessed epitopes that are inaccessible to monoclonal antibodies, and exhibit increased tissue penetration (e.g., approximately twofold in a prostate cancer model) compared to monoclonal antibodies. VHH-based therapeutics, such as caplacizumab, envafolimab, and ozoralizumab, have been approved for various indications, including rheumatoid arthritis, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and advanced solid tumors. Furthermore, bispecific and multispecific antibodies can recognize two or more distinct epitopes. Bispecific antibodies, such as amivantamab, a bispecific antibody targeting both epidermal growth factor receptor and hepatocyte growth factor receptor (EGFR×MET), combine signaling blockade, receptor down-modulation, and immune effector engagement in a single molecule. Other bispecifics, including bispecific T cell engagers, facilitate novel spatial configurations by promoting synapse formation between T cells and cancer cells. Several bispecific antibody drugs have already been approved, such as blinatumomab (CD19xCD3; CD, cluster of differentiation) for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, epcoritamab (CD20xCD3ε) for diffuse large B cell lymphoma, with many more on the horizon. Bispecific antibodies are also being explored to enable crossing biological barriers by sequentially binding to different targets.

Antibody development involves several key stages: discovery, lead identification, in vitro optimization, and preclinical in vivo evaluation. At each stage, the number of therapeutic antibody candidates is narrowed from potentially thousands in the discovery phase to a single antibody that enters the clinic. Additionally, to produce a viable drug, lead antibody candidates must be optimized before entering the clinic. Although the focus is often on optimizing affinity, other antibody developability properties – polyreactivity (also known as non-specific binding or polyspecificity), self-association, folding stability, solubility, viscosity, immunogenicity and expression titer – need to be considered as well (Fig. 1). Optimization is a key step because poor developability properties can result in issues later in the pipeline, requiring more time and resources to amend and potentially terminating the campaign. However, optimization can also be a bottleneck in antibody development, particularly when time-consuming, resource-intensive methods are used.

Optimizing antibodies early in the discovery phase can reduce problems later in development. For example, selecting candidates with high affinity (e.g., subnanomolar dissociation constants) and desirable manufacturability properties at the hit-to-lead stage can accelerate development. However, there are typically hundreds to thousands of candidates in the early discovery phase, and methods that can process vast numbers of antibodies are needed to take advantage of this efficiency gain. Furthermore, many antibody properties are linked, positively or negatively, rendering single-parameter optimization efforts inefficient or futile. For example, an antibody with high-aggregation propensity can, in some cases, also exhibit high immunogenicity. Additionally, increasing affinity increases the risk of non-specific binding and self-association. Therefore, optimization involves balancing benefits and tradeoffs. Advances in methods, such as the use of designed antibody libraries with improved intrinsic properties and in vitro screening methods for identifying drug-like antibody candidates, have facilitated the identification of antibodies with favorable developability properties. Nonetheless, when attempting to optimize for multiple parameters simultaneously, the amount of required experimentation can quickly exceed the realm of feasibility. Multi-objective antibody optimization has long posed a difficult yet paramount challenge, enabling the discovery of high-affinity antibodies with desirable developability properties early in the discovery and optimization phases, thereby increasing the likelihood of successful clinical translation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) methods have been increasingly used to optimize antibodies, supplementing and even replacing experimentation (BOX 1). These computational methods are created using either physics- and structure-based approaches or supervised ML methods to predict the outputs of in vitro assays and to predict and optimize specific properties, such as affinity, stability, solubility, or polyreactivity(Table 1). Deep learning methods, such as protein language and inverse folding models, have also been applied to learn representations of antibody sequences and structures that can be used for downstream antibody engineering tasks (Table 2). In this Review, we discuss computational-guided antibody engineering for multi-objective optimization of existing antibodies for various properties. Additionally, emerging generative frameworks, including diffusion-based protein design methods, are advancing the prospect of de novo antibody design optimized across multiple parameters involving both function and developability.

## MULTI-OBJECTIVE OPTIMIZATION OF EXISTING ANTIBODIES

### Antibody co-optimization using sub-library generation and deep sequencing

The antibody discovery process is often associated with tradeoffs between different antibody properties. The most common in vitro antibody discovery platforms, phage and yeast-surface display, can be used for high-throughput screening of antibodies with high affinity and specificity. However, antibody developability properties are often evaluated after the production of selected clones in mammalian cells. During this evaluation process, further optimization of developability properties may be necessary, but is challenging to achieve owing to tradeoffs between affinity and developability, such as polyreactivity and stability. This optimization process is time-consuming and tedious, and it only allows evaluation of a limited number of clones. However, computational tools can be used to incorporate antibody developability considerations into library generation and screening strategies.

The challenges associated with optimization of developability properties can be addressed using mammalian cell-surface display to generate and sort antibody libraries, enabling ML-guided prediction of variants with high antigen affinity and specificity (Fig. 2A). For example, a sub-library of a template antibody, trastuzumab, was generated by mutating heavy-chain complementary-determining region 3 (HCDR3), the region most often associated with antigen specificity. This library was then screened by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), and the binding and non-binding populations were deep sequenced. Enrichment ratios from the deep sequencing data were used to inform the rational design of a sub-library with more restricted diversity. The rationally designed sub-library was then sorted by FACS, and the binding and non-binding populations were deep sequenced again. Next, multiple ML algorithms were trained on deep sequencing data to predict clones with higher or similar antigen affinity relative to trastuzumab (KD of ~4×10−10 M) and those with much weaker affinity, as verified via biolayer interferometry. The best-performing model was a convolutional neural network, which was experimentally assessed. Lastly, in a process akin to in vivo clonal selection, the predicted antibody variants were filtered for properties such as net charge and hydrophobicity index to account for viscosity and in vivo clearance, as well as for solubility and immunogenicity. This led to the identification of redesigned antibodies with a range of affinities and improved biophysical properties compared to trastuzumab. This approach demonstrates the feasibility of antibody co-optimization by generating libraries directly using mammalian cells and filtering for developability properties. However, this method is computationally and experimentally intensive and, therefore, not ideal for more expansive antibody discovery campaigns, such as those involving multiple complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) and the optimization of multiple properties.

One common goal during antibody optimization is to improve biophysical properties, such as reducing polyreactivity while maintaining high affinity and bioactivity. However, because heavy-chain CDRs shape the antigen-binding site, mutations in these regions can alter hydrophobic and charged surface patches that drive non-specific interactions, creating strong tradeoffs between affinity and polyreactivity. To address this challenge, an ML model was developed to co-optimize binding affinity and polyreactivity (Fig. 2B). Using emibetuzumab, a clinical-stage antibody that exhibits high levels of non-specific binding, as a case study, a large yeast surface display sub-library (107 – 108 variants) was generated by introducing up to eight mutations per antibody in the heavy-chain CDRs at solvent-exposed positions enriched in hydrophobic or positively charged residues, which are predicted to mediate non-specific binding. The library was then sorted for strong and weak binders to both the target antigen and polyreactivity reagents. The sorted library was then deep sequenced to identify clones with high affinity (top 50% antigen-positive) versus low affinity, and with high polyreactivity (top 25%) versus low polyreactivity (bottom 10%) to polyspecificity reagents. Deep sequencing data was used to build an enriched dataset of 4000 sequences and to train simple ML models, including linear discriminant analysis (LDA). The LDA model projects high-dimensional (one-hot encoded) features onto a continuous one-dimensional space, thereby optimizing classification accuracy. These models could predict not only interclass differences, such as high vs. low affinity, but also intraclass differences, such as high vs. very high affinity. Therefore, these simple LDA models were used to project the affinity and polyreactivity of each sequence onto 2D plots and directly identify co-optimized variants along the Pareto frontier.

Next, the models were used to predict emibetuzumab variants with high affinity and low polyreactivity beyond the Pareto frontier – the set of undominated variants defining the tradeoff boundary between affinity and polyreactivity – in mutational space. LDA models trained on deep learning-based Unified Representation (UniRep) features, which are sequence embeddings from a pretrained recurrent neural network (mLSTM) trained on large protein sequence databases, outperform similar models trained with conventional physicochemical descriptors in terms of successfully generalizing predictions to variants with novel mutations. This approach enabled the discovery of emibetuzumab variants with higher affinity and reduced polyreactivity, surpassing the properties of variants in the original dataset. Clinically, these improvements could enable more effective, better-tolerated dosing regimens by increasing on-target potency while reducing off-target liabilities.

This approach integrates experimental and computational frameworks, combining deep sequencing, ML, and high-throughput experimental techniques to co-optimize therapeutic antibody variants. Furthermore, the study provides a blueprint for exploring novel mutational spaces and for predicting co-optimal variants beyond the Pareto frontier defined by the original dataset. The key strength of this method lies in the simultaneous optimization of multiple antibody properties, which requires precise prediction of both interclass and intraclass differences. Rather than relying on complex non-linear models, a relatively simple linear ML model is effective for analyzing large combinatorial sequence spaces and predicting antibody properties with sufficiently high accuracy (~93%) to be useful for real-world protein engineering applications.

Traditional antibody screening approaches can only explore limited regions of sequence space, typically screening dozens to thousands of variants from single-site or few-site-focused CDR libraries, which yield antibodies with suboptimal binding affinity and developability properties. Furthermore, focusing solely on improving affinity can negatively affect developability properties. One method enables the exploration of broader mutational space in combination with deep learning models to predict co-optimized antibody variants with high affinity and naturalness (Fig. 2C). The first step is to generate sub-libraries of a template antibody, trastuzumab, which are designed for an Activity-specific Cell-Enrichment assay, a high-throughput screening method for measuring the binding affinity of intracellularly expressed fragment antibody binding region (Fab) fragments in bacteria. This technology enables the generation of large sub-libraries of trastuzumab variants and, therefore, the exploration of broad mutational spaces. The first of three sub-libraries generated, library #1, contained >8,000 variants with up to 2 mutations in HCDR3, providing sufficient data to train predictive models despite a high prevalence of low-affinity binders. Library #2 was a subset of >200 sequences from library #1 with a distribution of binding affinities that were re-screened using Surface Plasmon Resonance (SPR), a label-free, real-time binding assay. Using the Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach (RoBERTa) architecture, antibody-specific protein language models were trained on sequences extracted from the Observed Antibody Space (OAS), a curated public database with over 1 billion annotated antibody sequences. The models were then fine-tuned using task-specific affinity data from library #1 and library #2, resulting in predicted affinities with relatively high accuracy (~87% of predictions were within ~3-fold of the measured KD by SPR) and generalization to unseen variants, with most of the novel variants showing improved binding compared to the parental trastuzumab. Finally, library #3 expanded the mutational space to >50,000 variants with triple mutations across HCDR2 and HCDR3, where the model successfully identified high-affinity binders, demonstrating its ability to predict variants within more complex mutational landscapes.

Furthermore, the language models pre-trained on the OAS database were used to compute naturalness scores across the entire mutational space. Naturalness was broadly correlated with key antibody developability properties, including immunogenicity and expression titers. Conversely, naturalness decreased with increasing mutational load. Random screening of Library #3 revealed that only 0.12% of variants exhibited both higher affinity and naturalness than the wild type, emphasizing the rarity of co-optimal candidates in an expanded mutational space. However, an exhaustive search that enumerates and scores the entire mutational space (~6.7 million variants) showed that co-optimal candidates are extremely rare: only ~0.06% are predicted to improve affinity while maintaining or improving naturalness, making this approach computationally intensive and not scalable. To accelerate in silico screening, a genetic algorithm was developed that iteratively refines sequences by combining affinity and naturalness models to select the best candidates. The genetic algorithm mimics natural selection by evolving a population of sequences over multiple generations, using selection, crossover, and mutation to optimize properties. The genetic algorithm performs nearly as well as an exhaustive search of the entire set of millions of sequences, achieving relatively high agreement (85% overlap with top 100) with exhaustive search results after just twenty generations using only 4,000 sequences. The algorithm’s iterative process efficiently narrows the search space, identifying rare, optimal variants more effectively than exhaustive sampling, demonstrating the ability of genetic algorithms to balance tradeoffs between affinity and naturalness.

This study provides a roadmap for exploring a broader mutational space using high-throughput assays to train deep learning models that predict high-affinity antibody variants. Additionally, a language model trained on natural antibody repertoires is used to evaluate the naturalness of antibody variants. Combined with a genetic algorithm, this method can effectively identify antibody variants with high affinity and naturalness. Future applications of this method include co-optimizing additional properties, such as addressing antigen-escape variants, improving specificity, and enhancing species cross-reactivity. These applications could enhance therapeutic antibody design and address challenges in identifying co-optimal antibody variants in diverse mutational and functional landscapes.

### Direct prediction of co-optimal antibody variants

Antibodies of non-human origin typically require humanization before entering the clinic to increase compatibility in humans and reduce the risk of immunogenicity. Many successful therapeutics have been humanized using CDR grafting, wherein non-human CDRs are grafted onto a human framework. Additionally, computational approaches for antibody humanization include the use of language models and germlining, though these approaches can compromise antibody function and/or stability. Machine learning has been used to humanize antibodies of non-human origin. However, in silico humanization methods typically depend on either selecting human frameworks primarily based on homology or using common human frameworks based on previous success with unrelated antibodies, both of which can result in tradeoffs between affinity and other developability properties. Although low humanness increases the risk for immunogenicity, developability issues such as antibody aggregation can also lead to undesirable immune responses, including the production of antidrug antibodies. Despite these tradeoffs, antibody humanization methods often do not rigorously consider additional developability properties when suggesting novel frameworks or humanizing mutations.

To develop antibodies with high humanness without sacrificing other developability properties, Computational hUMan AntiBody design (CUMab) uses energy-based ranking to co-optimize antibody humanness and stability with diverse human frameworks instead of more conventional homology-based humanization designs (Fig. 3A). CUMab, a one-shot optimization model, combines human Variable (V) and Joining (J) genes, DNA segments that recombine to create antibodies, to create over thousands of potential human frameworks to which CDRs of the target antibody are grafted. The model then calculates the energy of the grafted CDR-framework designs using the Rosetta all-atom energy function. Clones with favorable Rosetta energies are then selected to be experimentally evaluated. The model was validated by humanizing four murine antibodies – one with a crystal structure and three with computationally-predicted Fv structures. In all cases, the CUMab-designed humanized antibody variants had similar binding affinities and comparable or higher folding stability to the parental antibody.

To increase humanness further, another strategy, named specificity-determining residue (SDR) grafting, was evaluated, in which only residues in direct contact with the antigen were preserved and grafted. Higher sequence identity and superior biophysical properties were achieved with SDR grafting than with CDR grafting, but at the cost of reduced affinity. This strategy highlights the tradeoff between affinity, humanness, and other biophysical properties. Four out of five humanized antibodies in this study lacked sequences identifiable by conventional sequence homology-based methods. Reliance on structural rather than sequence homology sets this humanization method apart. Additionally, this one-shot optimization approach reduces the experimental burden of library construction, screening, and next-generation sequencing.

Similar to humanization, tradeoffs also exist between affinity interactions, such as antibody-antigen interactions, and non-affinity interactions, such as non-specific or self-interactions. Increasing the affinity of an antibody often comes with the price of increased self-association and polyreactivity. A systematic study of clinical-stage antibodies led to the development of ML models that maintain affinity interactions while minimizing non-affinity interactions (Fig. 3B). In this study, 80 clinical-stage antibodies were evaluated for self-association using the Charge-Stabilized Self-Interaction Nanoparticle Spectroscopy (CS-SINS) assay and for polyreactivity using the PolySpecificity Particle (PSP)assay. The CS-SINS assay measures antibody self-association under standard formulation conditions (pH 6, 10 mM histidine), and the PSP assay measures polyreactivity in physiological-like conditions (pH 7.4, PBS). The assayed antibodies were then grouped into four classes, namely Class I antibodies with low self-association and low polyreactivity (co-optimal), Class II with high self-association and low polyreactivity, Class III antibodies with high polyreactivity and low self-association, and Class IV antibodies with high self-association and high polyreactivity. Gaussian Naïve Bayes classifiers trained on up to three structural features derived from homology models were then used to develop two interpretable ML models that predict each developability property. The first model, trained on the CS-SINS dataset, identified that electrostatic properties, including Fv charge and ionic patch properties, were the key determinant of self-association. The second model, trained on the PSP dataset, revealed that the distributions of hydrophobic and ionic patches were the primary determinants of polyreactivity.

Leveraging these insights, three clinical-stage antibodies with suboptimal biophysical properties, namely panitumumab (Class II), gantenerumab (Class III), and cinpanemab (Class IV), were co-optimized as a proof-of-principle. First, single-site mutations were selected from conserved residues outside the antigen-binding site. Iterative cycles of homology modeling and ML predictions were then employed to introduce 2–6 mutations per variant. Multi-site variants were generated with mutations in both the framework and CDRs. Experimental validation revealed that all variants exhibit reduced self-association or non-specific binding compared to the respective original antibodies. Twelve of 17 variants were classified as Class I co-optimized antibodies, and 9 had affinities similar to or better than those of the parental antibodies.

Previous work used complex deep-learning models trained on large protein datasets, relying on the generation and deep sequencing of antibody libraries. In contrast, this study uses data on antibody structural features to train interpretable ML models, enabling direct prediction of co-optimized antibody variants. This report outlines a scalable and predictive tool that streamlines the selection of lead antibodies and guides the rational co-optimization of developability and functionality.

Stability and solubility are two other key determinants in the developability of a lead antibody. For example, high-concentration formulations (greater than 100 mg/mL) are crucial for subcutaneous administration but are not possible for many antibodies owing to poor solubility. Similarly, conformational stability impacts product quality, shelf life, and routes of administration. Co-optimizing an antibody for both stability and solubility can be a lengthy and expensive process, often requiring extensive experimentation. However, an integrated computational workflow for co-optimizing antibody variants for solubility and conformational stability while maintaining binding affinity can reduce the time and cost of this process (Fig. 3C). This workflow requires both structural and sequence information of the antibody as inputs. The structural data is fed into CamSol, which identifies residues linked to poor solubility and aggregation as well as candidate mutation sites. Simultaneously, the antibody sequence is used to generate a position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM) to identify highly conserved residues that remain fixed and poorly conserved residues as candidate mutation sites. Then, amino acid substitutions permitted by a specified PSSM conservation threshold are made for each candidate mutation site. Next, the single amino acid mutants are assigned an intrinsic solubility score by CamSol and a stability score compared to wild type (ΔΔG) by the energy function FoldX. Top single amino acid mutations with improved solubility and stability are then combined and screened again for any further improvements in stability and solubility before a panel of co-optimal variants is generated. The resultant panel antibodies were corroborated experimentally using several parental antibodies, demonstrating relatively high prediction accuracy (66–84%), with most variants having comparable or higher stability and solubility to the wild type while maintaining affinity. Some compromises were made in the interest of developing a leaner workflow, including limiting the number of analyzed mutation combinations, which decreases computational burden at the cost of sampling all possible permutations of combined mutations. Overall, this workflow integrates solubility and stability optimization into a single, easy-to-use web tool and could reduce time and cost for generating co-optimal antibody variants for stability and solubility. Furthermore, this method is applicable to diverse types of antibodies, including those from llama VHHs, human antibodies, and non-immunoglobulin proteins.

## TOWARD DE NOVO DESIGN OF CO-OPTIMIZED ANTIBODIES

Although computational methods have been explored for antibody co-optimization, the de novo design of antigen-specific antibodies with co-optimized affinities and developability properties remains extremely challenging. In this Review, de novo antibody design refers to the process of designing either novel antibody CDRs or antibody variable regions against a given target, without using initial or template antibody CDRs or variable regions specific to the same target.

As a step toward de novo design coupled with antibody co-optimization, a computational design and filtering strategy has been used to identify high-affinity antibody variants with favorable developability properties (Fig. 4a). The strategy was tested by optimizing antibodies targeting the receptor-binding domain of the SARS-CoV-2 virus. First, panels of antibody variants were identified using three approaches: database scanning, an inverse folding model, and protein language models. Two of the design approaches, based on inverse folding and protein language models, yielded promising variants. The protein language model approach aimed to improve biophysical properties of existing antigen-specific antibodies while maintaining high affinity. A panel of variants was generated by mutating CDRs using a combination of sequence-based protein language models and physics-based scoring methods (such as Rosetta). Potential mutations were identified using an ensemble of protein language models, and Rosetta was used to accept or reject the suggested mutations. The inverse folding model approach aimed to expand binding specificity towards additional SARS-CoV-2 variants, and a panel of variants was designed using an inverse folding model. Paratope residues were identified using predicted structures of the antibody-antigen complexes, and the four CDRs with the most paratope residues were selected for mutagenesis. Paratope residues within these CDRs were mutated according to suggestions from an antibody message passing neural network (AbMPNN), an antibody-specific inverse folding model.

Following both approaches, a filtering strategy was introduced to select antibody variants for experimental evaluation. First, antibody sequences with motifs associated with poor developability were removed from further consideration. Second, the Therapeutic Antibody Profiler (TAP) was used to remove variants with structural properties associated with poor developability. TAP is a tool that compares the biophysical properties, including the total CDR length, hydrophobic and electrostatic patches, and structural charge symmetry, with the distribution of clinical stage antibodies. An antibody is assigned a green, amber, or red flag, representing low, medium, or high developability risk, based on where its biophysical properties fall within the distribution of clinical-stage antibodies. Next, computationally predicted antibody-antigen complexes were evaluated using Rosetta, and variants with unfavorable interactions between the antibody and antigen were removed. Finally, the remaining structures were ranked using the Rosetta score and predicted change in free energy.

Using this computational design and filtering strategy, developable antibodies with affinity for multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants were successfully identified. For example, an antibody with poor developability was used as a starting point for the protein-language model strategy. All designs tested (12) showed reduced aggregation propensity relative to the parental antibody, and most of the designs (10 of 12) had improved thermostability. Additionally, all antibody multisite mutants retained binding to multiple SARS-CoV-2 variants, demonstrating that the design and filtering strategy identified variants co-optimal for affinity and developability. The inverse folding model design approach also showed promise in identifying co-optimal variants. Antibodies optimized using this method had desirable biophysical properties but could bind only to a single viral variant. Using mutations predicted by the inverse folding model, the investigators identified nine variants of two parental antibodies that showed at least moderate binding to all viral variants tested, low aggregation propensity, and high thermostability. Although short of truly de novo design, as the authors did not generate entirely novel CDRs or Fv sequences, this strategy demonstrated in silico design and filtering approaches that could be used to identify co-optimal antibodies.

Separately, a different fragment-based strategy for computational antibody design was reported that does not use protein language and inverse folding models (Fig. 4B). To start, an antibody-antigen database of CDR-like fragments and their associated antigen-like fragments was extracted from the Protein Data Bank and Structural Antibody Database. CDR fragments were identified as linear motifs found on any protein that resemble CDRs, and antigen-like regions were defined as residues that interact with the CDR fragments.

Next, a model was developed that uses the structure of a target epitope as input and searches the antibody-antigen database for antigen-like regions that match parts of the epitope. CDR-like fragments were then retrieved, superimposed, and joined with other pairs of antigen-like regions and CDR-like fragments to form contiguous CDR motifs. Side chain optimization was then carried out to maximize favorable interactions between the contiguous CDR motif and the antigen. This method typically yields multiple CDR motif designs, ranked by the number of favorable interactions and the CamSol solubility score. Top-ranked CDR motifs were then matched and combined with existing CDRs and antibodies from the Structural Antibody Database as full CDRs or combinatorially with either more than one motif per CDR loop or multiple CDR motifs across different CDR loops. In parallel, an alternative grafting method was employed, in which CDR motifs were grafted directly onto a well-characterized, loop-replacement-tolerant scaffold.

As a proof-of-concept, this fragment-based method was used to generate de novo nanobodies against human serum albumin, yielding three designs that were well folded and highly stable, with modest (submicromolar) binding affinities against two distinct epitopes. Similarly, two nanobodies against the receptor-binding domain of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein were generated with submicromolar affinity that competed with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) binding. Furthermore, to benchmark the design strategy, the method was run on a collection of antigens with diverse sequences and structures to find high epitope coverage, demonstrating that this strategy could generate diverse antibody designs against a wide range of epitopes. Lastly, to assess the method’s applicability, AlphaFold2-generated antigen structures were used as inputs in place of experimentally determined ones, and the resulting nanobodies were mostly identical to those generated using experimentally determined antigen structures. This demonstrates that the method is compatible with antigen structures determined both experimentally and computationally.

This fragment-based method represents a distinct design philosophy from the previously discussed strategies. By matching the target epitope with existing protein structures and linear motifs that interact with them, this method can generate de novo CDRs by combining existing CDR-like fragments and yield well-folded and stable antigen-specific antibodies while screening as few as one to three variants. Furthermore, this strategy is not reliant on experimentally-determined epitope structures, as AlphaFold2-predicted antigen structures can be used, broadening its applicability. However, the nanobodies generated in the proof-of-concept studies had modest (submicromolar) affinity, necessitating further optimization to yield higher-affinity lead antibodies. Furthermore, it is unknown how this method would apply to larger, multidomain antigen-binding (Fv) regions, which are necessary for full monoclonal antibody design, rather than nanobodies, especially with respect to the CDR-grafting strategy. Nevertheless, this fragment-based design method can generate co-optimized lead antibodies in hours to days with broadly accessible computing resources and could be useful for generating novel antibodies against specific epitopes or difficult targets.

The third strategy aimed at de novo design of co-optimal antibodies uses a diffusion model, named RFdiffusion, to predict antibody structures that bind to a predefined epitope (Fig. 4C). Diffusion models generate data by learning to denoise datasets that are intentionally corrupted by introduced Gaussian noise. Previously established for predicting protein structures, RFdiffusion has been fine-tuned for predicting the structures of antibody-antigen complexes. In this strategy, the sequence and structure of the antibody framework were fixed, and the goal was to generate de novo CDRs. The framework was defined as a VHH or single-chain antibody fragment (scFv), and the antibody model could freely rotate to accommodate the docking mode dictated by RFdiffusion. Furthermore, a specific epitope on the antigen was specified to guide CDR generation for the target epitope. After RFdiffusion generated a docked antibody structure, an inverse folding model, ProteinMPNN, was used to design the de novo CDR loop sequences. A fine-tuned version of RoseTTAFold2 was used to predict the structures of RFdiffusion-designed antibodies for design filtering and model validation. Using a humanized VHH framework for model validation, the RFdiffusion-based workflow was used to generate de novo VHHs against six distinct targets. VHH designs for each target were screened with either yeast-surface display (thousands of designs per target) or E. coli expression and SPR (approximately a hundred designs per target). The best variants achieved affinities ranging from tens of nanomolar to micromolar for their respective targets, with some designs exhibiting novel binding modes. As in the previously discussed studies, this model and workflow must be improved before any viable drug-like antibodies can be reliably generated. Further optimization in affinity and developability properties must be performed on antibodies generated using this diffusion-modeling-based method. Overall, the application of diffusion modeling in antibody design opens another avenue for the de novo generation of antibodies.

## Outlook

AI and ML could ultimately be used for de novo antibody design against targets that are both high-value and difficult to target with conventionally developed antibodies. For example, membrane proteins such as GPCRs and ion channels have high therapeutic value, as they are a highly diverse family of proteins, serve important biological functions, and can be useful biomarkers, but these are complex antigens with little extracellular surface area for antibody binding. Producing membrane protein antigens often requires detergent-solubilization, or expression on nanodiscs, liposomes, or virus-like particles. However, preserving the native conformation and relevance for antibody generation with these methods is challenging. Therefore, de novo design efforts are needed to circumvent these challenges and enable antibody design against difficult antigens. Although recent advances have been made in antibody generation against GPCRs, these efforts have been plagued by low success rates and heavy reliance on experimental screening to identify successful designs, and these approaches have been validated on relatively few targets, such as the four targets discussed among de novo design methods in this Review. To address these issues, the scientific community must have broader access to de novo design methods to adequately test them and define the problems to which they should and/or can be applied.

One of the greatest bottlenecks to building AI and ML models is access to large amounts of high-quality data and the associated costs of generating it (BOX 2). Scientists rely on relatively modest amounts of data released by companies or universities. These include datasets with 10s-100s of continuous measurements from in vitro assays or larger datasets with 1000s of binary-labeled samples. Although many such datasets are invaluable to the field, efforts to promote widespread data sharing and collaboration are essential to grow the computational antibody design space and to democratize the antibody engineering field. The AIntibody competition offers a model for data sharing and collaboration. This competition is designed to benchmark novel computational methods by inviting research groups worldwide to apply their methods and perform the same task within the same time constraints. In addition to being compared to one another, the computational predictions and/or designs are compared with those of established experimental methods, providing a direct performance comparison between AI and/or computational methods and established technology. This type of collaboration and data sharing is crucial in elucidating the capabilities and limitations of AI and computational methods.

Computational scientists often need to extract data from studies designed for other purposes or settle for data that does not align with the objectives of their models. In response, considerable effort has been put into improving computational models to enable training with imperfect or sparse data. For example, meta learning can be used to enable model training with noisy and under-labeled data, demonstrating that AI and ML can bridge the gap between experimental data collection and model requirements. However, as AI and ML models become increasingly specialized and data-hungry, experimental data collection should align with their requirements. Considerations for data curation in antibody engineering include the appropriateness of the assay choice, technical reproducibility, and the balance of the datasets. For example, the strategy of identifying negative samples has had a large impact on ML models in antibody engineering. Particular attention should be paid to curating ML datasets with sufficient positive and negative training data, which runs counter to traditional experimental screening methods that prioritize selecting the best-performing proteins.

To generate high-quality models, computational scientists need to design experiments and collect data specifically for the model they are developing. This is most relevant for studies in which data generation and model development go hand in hand. Although improving the collection of affinity and specificity datasets can be achieved through conventional methods, collecting other developability datasets for multi-objective optimization poses a challenge. Developability properties such as viscosity, solubility, aggregation, and pharmacokinetics are harder to measure at the scales required for AI and ML model training, necessitating high-throughput assay development. Furthermore, protein language models can be used to improve antibody design and multi-objective optimization. For example, protein language models are useful for affinity maturation despite lacking information about specific antigen or antibody properties. Such models could potentially efficiently reduce the search space for mutations that are not only native-like but also functional. Additionally, integrating protein structural information has been found to improve correlations between language model-predicted likelihoods and certain antibody properties, such as antibody affinity, compared to sequence-only models. However, many language models are trained on non-antibody proteins, which are generally not drug-like, and not all developability properties are readily linked to intrinsic antibody properties predicted by these models. The capabilities and limitations of using such language models for multi-objective optimization must be defined, especially for antibody properties beyond affinity, stability, and humanness.
